newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Suffering Russia protests but revolt unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Suffering Russia protests but revolt unlikely.

text.p: Russia's day of protest against unpaid wages brought tens of thousands onto the streets, but the patience and fatalism of ordinary people should ensure there is no mass uprising against the state, analysts said on Thursday.

Once the red flags and Lenin banners are furled and put away after Soviet-style marches in cities across the country, the main question remains unanswered -- how long will the government take to break out of economic crisis?

The answer appears to be in the hands of the new-look government headed by veteran Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. He announced confidently on Wednesday that his new team of ministers "know what to do and how to do it."
But sceptics recall his own admission some time ago when he described a previous attempt to improve things by saying: "We wanted to make things better but the result was the same as always."

Protests by people who have not been paid for months are hardly surprising and nearly all politicians -- from President Boris Yeltsin to the communist opposition, from regional governors to industry bosses -- have used it for their own goals, saying the action was quite justified.
Yeltsin used it as an excuse to reshuffle the government. The new team of liberal ministers has said only consistent reforms can resolve the crisis.

The trade unions, trying to find a role for themselves in the post-communist era, are taking the opportunity to boost their own image. But they all but dropped their central demand for the government's resignation after the reshuffle.
The communist-led opposition, ceding the central role to the unions up to Thursday, used the day itself to demand a radical change of policy. It is unlikely to happen.

The hardline communist daily Sovietskaya Rossiya, accused the Kremlin of "genocide against the nation". It declared: "Law and truth are on our side. All Russia is behind us and we have nowhere to run. Those who don't like our anger can only flee."
Many employers, blaming authorities rather than their own incompetence, are likely to demand more state help.
Regional bosses, many of them opposed to the Kremlin, are backing the protests and will use them as a lever in their attempts to wrest more power and money from central government.
Barring a mass explosion of violence similar to that in Albania this month, the protest may even help some of the impoverished millions to survive for some more time.
In typical last-minute style, the Kremlin dispatched billions of roubles to many regions and working groups to pay back some of the salaries and pensions at the very last moment.
Early reports made no mention of disturbances, though some opposition figures, like popular general Alexander Lebed, have warned about a coming "Russian riot, cruel and merciless."
There are individual cases of desperation -- an unpaid father of five hanged himself in Yaroslavl because he could not feed his family.
But on a wider scale, the legendary patience that has seen the Russian people through centuries of hardship seems bottomless.

"The people are not getting ready to riot, they are just waiting," wrote observer Galina Kovalskaya in the influential Itogi weekly magazine. "They expect that this mess will, in some miraculous way, transform itself into order, all by itself."
Kovalskaya quoted one trade union leader as saying: "It appears that the president and the premier also believe, deep in their hearts, that everything will somehow turn out all right."
